# Sharp arithmetic peak-Bonnesen comparison for cap profiles

This is a proved volume comparison, not a deterministic-center theorem.
It strengthens the two preceding arithmetic mass inequalities. The proof
is a normalized layer-cake argument and an elementary distinct-sum count.
Independent audit is pending.

The ordinary maximal-section Bonnesen inequality suggested the normalized
level argument; its standard continuous statement and proof appear in
[Böröczky and Serra, Remarks on the equality case of the Bonnesen inequality,
Theorem1.2 and Section3.2](https://www.renyi.hu/~carlos/bonnesen-high-equa-pub.pdf).
The arithmetic statement below is proved directly rather than cited from
that paper. No OC result or status was searched for.

## 1. Exact statement

Let d>=1. For i=1,...,k let A_i be a nonempty finite union of compact
convex fibers in R^n times R^d with integer bases, positive mixed mass
M_i, and largest positive fiber volume a_i. Ignore any zero-volume input
fibers, or include them only as enlargements of the output below. Let
lambda_i>0, sum_i lambda_i=1, and suppose every base combination
sum_i lambda_i p_i of positive input fibers is integral. Define

    T=sum_i lambda_i A_i,
    L=sum_i lambda_i a_i^(1/d),
    R=sum_i M_i/a_i-k+1.

Then

    mu(T) >= R L^d.                                  (1)

Here T-fibers are finite unions of compact convex sets; they need not
be convex, and are measured as unions. All counts in the proof are of
distinct output bases. In particular no coincident contributions are
added within a fiber.

For two midpoint inputs in the same parity class,

    mu((A+B)/2) >= (M_A/a+M_B/b-1)
                         ((a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))/2)^d.     (2)

The factor is the SUM of the two effective counts minus one, with no
extra balance or scale-ratio hypothesis. Each effective count is at
least one, so (2) improves the earlier maximum-of-two-counts bound.

## 2. Proof by normalized volume levels

For 0<t<=1 let P_i(t) be the bases whose input fiber volume is at least
t a_i, and let N_i(t)=|P_i(t)|. Each such set is nonempty because its
largest-volume fiber is included. For every choice p_i in P_i(t), the
output fiber at sum_i lambda_i p_i contains their Minkowski combination.
Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski in dimension d gives its volume at least

    (sum_i lambda_i (t a_i)^(1/d))^d=t L^d.          (3)

For finite nonempty sets in a real vector space,

    |sum_i lambda_i P_i(t)| >= sum_i N_i(t)-k+1.     (4)

For two sets, list both in increasing order of a linear functional
injective on each. Use all sums with the first point of the first set,
followed by the sums of the remaining points of that set with the last
point of the second set. These form a strictly increasing list of length
N_1+N_2-1. Applying this repeatedly proves (4). Positive scaling is
injective and hence does not change the input counts.

All the output bases in (4) are integer by hypothesis. The number of
T-fibers of volume at least t L^d is therefore at least its right side.
The layer-cake formula, restricting the output integral to [0,L^d], gives

    mu(T) >= L^d integral_0^1 [sum_i N_i(t)-k+1] dt
           =L^d [sum_i M_i/a_i-k+1].

The last equality is the finite sum of the elementary identities
integral_0^1 1_(v>=t a_i) dt=v/a_i. This proves (1). The values at
finitely many volume thresholds and at t=0 do not affect the integral.
No convexity of the overall base union or of the overall source is
required for this argument; convexity is used inside each input fiber.

## 3. Relation to the previous corrected Brunn--Minkowski bound

For c_i in[0,1] with sum_i c_i=k-1, put S_i=M_i/a_i-c_i>=0. Then
sum_i S_i=R. Hölder's inequality with conjugate exponents (d+1)/d and
d+1 gives

    sum_i lambda_i^(d/(d+1))(M_i-c_i a_i)^(1/(d+1))
      =sum_i (lambda_i a_i^(1/d))^(d/(d+1)) S_i^(1/(d+1))
      <= L^(d/(d+1)) R^(1/(d+1)).

Thus (1) implies every inequality in
`candidate 04cc8e0ae0c3cab6`. That earlier
rearrangement proof remains valid, including its endpoint treatment,
but it is numerically superseded here. Its balance condition was needed
only to make its Hölder bound attain R L^d, not for (1) itself.

Also R>=M_i/a_i for each i. It follows that

    mu(T)^(1/d) >= R^(1/d)L
                 >=sum_i lambda_i M_i^(1/d),        (5)

recovering the same-coset root comparison. For k=m identical sources,
lambda_i=1/m, it gives exactly m M-(m-1)a. The dimension-sensitive
Ehrhart refinement for an actual convex body's equal-threshold levels
is separate and can still be stronger in higher base rank.

## 4. Application to every parallel ambient cap family

Let C be an actual compact convex body and ell any affine functional
on its full ambient space. Take A_i to be the positive-volume fibers
in specified residue classes of C intersect {ell>=t_i}. When their
weighted base combinations are integral, convexity implies

    T subset C intersect {ell>=sum_i lambda_i t_i}.

Consequently (1) bounds the ACTUAL mass of the cap on the right from
below, using the masses and peaks of the input residue-restricted caps.
This includes oblique ell and closed vertical caps carrying boundary
mass. If one input cap has zero mixed mass, the displayed formula with
division by a_i is not applied; that case needs a separate zero-mass
statement if it is used in another argument.

For the common-parity midpoint application, write
F_r(t)=mu(C intersect {ell>=t} intersect (r+2Z^n times R^d)) and let
a_r(t) be its largest cap-fiber volume. Whenever both input masses
are positive, (2) gives the explicit profile inequality

    F((s+t)/2) >= [F_r(s)/a_r(s)+F_r(t)/a_r(t)-1]
                     [(a_r(s)^(1/d)+a_r(t)^(1/d))/2]^d,       (6)

where F is the cap mass over ALL integer fibers. No assertion that
F_r itself is concave is made.

## 5. Sharpness and boundaries of the claim

Let k=m, lambda_i=1/m, let K be any d-dimensional convex body of
volume one, and choose integers N_i>=1 and numbers r_i>0. Take source i
with bases 0,m,...,m(N_i-1) on one primitive integer line and every fiber
equal to r_i K. Then M_i=N_i r_i^d and a_i=r_i^d. Every output base is
an integer from zero to sum_i(N_i-1), and every output fiber is exactly
(sum_i r_i/m)K. Therefore

    mu(T)=(sum_i N_i-k+1)(sum_i r_i/m)^d,

which is equality in (1). This also includes single-fiber inputs and
all unequal count and scale ratios. Closed fiber boundaries do not
change any of these d-volume identities.

The arithmetic integrality condition is essential: the generated bases
must belong to the measured lattice. Applying (1) to an arbitrary
sampling set would incorrectly count missing intermediate fibers.
Different residue-class applications can generate the same output
bases, so their bounds cannot be added. Finally, (6) relates cap
profiles for a fixed normal; it does not provide one point with a
simultaneous lower bound in every normal. That remains the OC task.

## 6. Intrinsic-measure version inside the original convex body

The same comparison is valid with intrinsic H_q when the inputs lie in
the original S=C intersect (Z^n times R^d), q=dim_H(S)>=1, provided
M_i and a_i use H_q and only positive H_q fibers are used. Replace d by
q in (1). Here is the direction check that is needed for that assertion.

Every integer fiber of C has affine dimension at most q, because S is
a finite union of those convex fibers and its Hausdorff dimension is
their maximum. A positive H_q input fiber has affine direction space
of dimension exactly q. For k>=2, take any one fiber from each source.
Their positive-weight Minkowski combination is contained in an integer
fiber of C. Its affine direction space is the sum of the input direction
spaces, since affine hull commutes with positive Minkowski combination.
That sum has dimension at most q. Each summand already has dimension q,
so all these spaces coincide. Holding one fiber in a different input
fixed and varying the first input proves that ALL positive input fibers
share one common q-dimensional direction space L.

Translate each input fiber into L, apply q-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski
there, and then translate its Minkowski output back by the weighted sum
of those translation vectors. Translations are isometries for H_q, so
the volume inequality (3) is unchanged with q in place of d. If several
combinations reach the same integer base, each resulting set is still
contained in its actual C-fiber; that fiber has dimension at most q.
The proof counts that output base once and uses only a lower bound on
its H_q measure. Thus neither differing affine origins nor output
collisions change the layer-cake argument. For k=1 the assertion is the
identity and no common-direction claim is needed.

For q=0, every nonempty convex integer fiber is a singleton and H_0 is
counting measure. The appropriate separate assertion is

    |sum_i lambda_i A_i| >= sum_i |A_i|-k+1,

under the same integral-output condition; this is exactly (4). No power
1/q is used. Nonempty lower-dimensional intersections therefore do not
require changing the measure in this auxiliary comparison.

The same common-direction argument applies to the equal-source residue
levels in `candidate 57e3e17a84fce5c1`, so its normalized
level-hull counting proof also extends to intrinsic H_q for q>=1. At
q=0 it is simply its lattice-point dilation statement. None of these
extensions supplies the missing center-selection implication.
